author: hoeschec
text:
Thinking a lot about IQM's lately.

How does an IQM happen? How can IT's ignore levels?

Do they place huge orders over a short amount of time to cause a gap in pricing?

Where do they place these orders?

Let's assume $100M of sell orders exists here. When price reaches the QM level it will bounce as long as there is less than $100M worth of buyers at that moment. If there is more than $100M of buyers price will consume the sell orders and price will rise. Price must consume the short orders before it can move beyond the level, right?

How are IT's able to 'skip over' these areas?

If IT's want to skip the level they need to create more buy orders. This causes price to move up. The theory behind trading the IQM (as I understand it) is price bounces at a previously ignored level because residual orders exist. But how can there be residual orders...aren't those orders consumed when price moves through the zone?

Maybe IT's create huge Buy orders to cause a gap to occur? If price changes rapidly there will be gap...trapping traders who can't execute quick enough.

To me, it seems like an IQM really just a liquidity gap that fills at a later date?

How do we define an IQM? What is the difference between a DM and an IQM? What if price comes close to the QM level but falls just short of the level. Does this count as a IQM? Often times price will miss the QM level by a few pips...do we still count this as an IQM?

During IF's video, he mentions "IQM" when there is no valid QM...I think there is a difference between an IQM and a IHS (Ignored head and shoulders). QM's have an engulf whereas H&S does not.

author: hoeschec
text:
Some drawings I made today

If I want to enter a long trade at the location indicated on the drawings, I want to buy at the best price possible. I wan to buy in the direction of the valid engulf. A valid engulf is an engulf that has yet to hit its target. Usually it is challenging to determine whether PA is depicting a FO or an EG. If I buy at the location indicated in my drawing, I need to make sure price is coming from an unmet target for longs.

In all of my drawings there is a grey line labeled "Opposing Zone". I think it is important to define what this opposing zone should be, in terms of the formation of a LS. My understanding (although I might be wrong) is a valid LS is formed after it engulfs a UFL/LFL. In this case, it shows price engulfing an opposing UFL.

Taking a closer look at this USD-JPY Trade. The more I Iook, the more I see:

If anyone sees something I missed please feel free to let me know!

1. Kink of LS #5 2. Established range, created by the kink formed at #1 3. Another LS forms, as final LS formed prior to a break of range #2 4. Strong momentum candle breaks range # 2

A - Engulf

5. LS 6. RBD 7. Another LTF IQM formed as price breaks through 8. Demand formed, creating a nice level to FO at a later time 9. "High" portion of a partially formed bullish QM 10. Engulf above established RS (# 9), and the "Higher High" Portion of the partially formed bullish QM

B - The entry long occurs at the important kink (hidden in large momentum candle to the left) and at the same time forms a DM.

My focus this week will be establishing a list of paramaters that I will use as a checklist to guide my decision making process. There will be two main kinds of parameters:

1. Parameters that must exist in order for me to take a trade 2. Parameters that specify 'aspects' of PA that can't exist in order for me to take a trade
